reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An acquired fibrosing disorder of skin and internal organs occurring almost exclusively in patients with severe renal impairment exposed to gadolinium-based contrast agents
Presents with symmetrical, progressive woody induration of the skin, most often on the lower limbs and forearms, with brawny hyperpigmentation and a cobblestoned, peau d'orange surface
Fibrosis leads to painful joint contractures and marked loss of mobility, and yellow scleral plaques may be seen in younger patients
Characteristically the face is spared, an important clue distinguishing it from scleroderma and scleromyxoedema

Risk is greatest with high-risk (linear, less stable) gadolinium agents, higher doses and repeated exposures in patients with an eGFR below about thirty or on dialysis, including those with acute kidney injury
Diagnosis combines the clinical picture with a deep skin biopsy showing spindle-cell proliferation with CD34-positive fibrocytes and thickened collagen, correlated with clinicoradiological criteria

Prevention is paramount: avoid or minimise high-risk contrast agents in advanced renal disease and prefer more stable macrocyclic agents; established disease is difficult to treat and may improve if renal function is restored
reference.pathophysiology: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is triggered by exposure to gadolinium-based contrast agents in the setting of markedly reduced renal clearance, which prolongs circulation of gadolinium and permits dissociation of the metal from its chelate (transmetallation), particularly with less stable linear agents. Retained gadolinium deposits in tissues and, together with uraemia and possibly other cofactors, is thought to recruit circulating CD34-positive, procollagen-positive bone-marrow-derived fibrocytes into the skin and other organs. These cells, driven by profibrotic cytokines such as transforming growth factor-beta, proliferate and deposit excess collagen and mucin, producing progressive dermal and systemic fibrosis that can involve muscle, lungs, heart and diaphragm.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic graft-versus-host disease with sclerodermatous features
additionalInvestigations: Deep incisional (including fascia) skin biopsy showing fibrocyte proliferation, thickened collagen bundles and mucin
Renal function including eGFR to confirm and stage kidney impairment
Review of gadolinium contrast exposure history, agent type and dose
Immunohistochemistry for CD34 highlighting spindle-cell fibrocytes
Autoimmune serology to help exclude systemic sclerosis and related disorders
Serum protein electrophoresis to exclude a paraproteinaemia mimicking scleromyxoedema
redFlags: Rapidly progressive skin thickening with developing joint contractures
Systemic fibrosis causing restrictive lung disease or cardiac involvement
Diaphragmatic involvement leading to respiratory compromise
Profound loss of mobility with dependency and risk of complications of immobility
reference.prognosis: The course is typically chronic and progressive with substantial disability from contractures and immobility, and systemic fibrosis contributes to mortality in severe cases. Some patients stabilise or improve when renal function recovers, for example after successful transplantation, but established fibrosis often persists.
pitfalls: Administering high-risk gadolinium agents to patients with advanced renal disease without recognising the risk
Mistaking the condition for systemic sclerosis and overlooking the characteristic sparing of the face
Taking too superficial a biopsy and missing the diagnostic deep dermal and fascial fibrosis
Failing to obtain a contrast exposure history in a dialysis patient with new skin induration
Assuming a single, low-dose exposure carries no risk in severe renal impairment
